newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Project offers hope to Kabul's children.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Project offers hope to Kabul's children.

text.p: Twelve-year-old Matine sits cross-legged on a grubby carpet, happily shovelling handfuls of bread soaked in bean soup into his mouth.
He wants to be a teacher when he grows up, he says between mouthfuls.

Not an unattainable ambition in the normal world, but for Matine the shoe-shine boy, who lives with his widowed mother and seven brothers and sisters in a single room in war-torn Kabul, it is almost beyond reach. Almost.

Matine was having lunch at a centre of the Aschiana programme. Aschiana, which means nest in Persian, was set up by the Swiss-based charity Terre des Hommes (TDH) to provide basic education and food in a secure environment for 250 street kids.
According to a TDH survey, 28,000 children between the ages of five and 14 work on the streets of Kabul, a city with a population estimated at one million.
Matine is typical of many of these children -- desperately short of opportunities, if not drive and ambition.
He says he earns 12,000 Afghanis (55 U.S. cents) on a good day shining shoes, a quarter of which goes to pay for polish and to hire the brushes and the wooden box he carries them in.
Even if schools re-open, he could not afford to attend.

Aschiana provides free classes in reading, writing, religious education, mathematics and personal hygiene. It also has vocational training classes in carpentry, carpet weaving, tailoring, and flower-making, among other things.

And it provides two meals a day, breakfast and lunch, which twice a week includes meat, and the chance to wash. "I like the breakfast and lunch," says Matine, adding after a little gentle prodding from his teacher that he likes the education as well.
NONE SKIP THE EDUCATION
Nick Hughes of TDH says that in theory the children could eat the meals and avoid the educational element, but none do so.

"No part of the Aschiana programme is compulsory. I could see kids turning up for the meals and then leaving, but none of them do this. Most stay for the whole programme, although many go out to work in the break between 12 and two," says Hughes.
Kabul children's hunger for knowledge is proportional to the level of destruction in the educational set-up.
The Taleban closed all schools when they took over Kabul six mnnths ago, but even before then the system was in dire straits.

Since the fall of the communists in 1992, schools have been destroyed and their contents looted. Teachers fled abroad to escape the fighting and those who stayed were not paid. Even when they were open, without text books, desks, chairs or blackboards, it was often too dangerous for pupils to attend.
"Because of the rocketing and bombing, parents were not ready to send their children out to school," says Mohammed Gul Wardaki of Aschiana.
Even today, when Kabul is free from rockets and air-raids, Aschiana, which receives $30,000 a year in aid funding, has no desks or chairs and no textbooks.
The children sit cross-legged on the ground laboriously copying from the blackboard into dog-eared exercise books. The teachers are paid the equivalent of $35 a month.
NO SCHOOLING FOR GIRLS
Kabul's educational establishments, including Aschiana, have also suffered from the Taleban's draconian decrees on women.
The militia's banning of women from the workplace cost Aschiana 30 percent of its teaching staff. The Taleban also closed girls' schools in parts of the country they control.

But Aschiana is the only school in Kabul so far to have avoided losing its girl pupils. Kabul University re-opened earlier this month without any of the 4,000 women students it had before the Taleban take-over.
The Taleban say they have no moral objection to girls' education up to the age of nine, but lack the resources to re-open the schools.
However, they have been reluctant to sign a protocol with the United Nations that offers U.N. funds to refurbish 20 Kabul schools, as long as half of them are for girls.
The disruption of the educational system has already created a generation who know little more than how to survive in a war zone, the so-called Kalashnikov generation.
Aschiana is trying to redress the balance.
Matine and his fellow street children at Aschiana represent a small glimmer of hope in an otherwise bleak future.
